question: Which of these statements about the 1967 elections is/are correct? (a) Congress won the Lok Sabha elections but lost the Assembly elections in many states. (b) Congress lost both Lok Sabha and Assembly elections. (c) Congress lost majority in the Lok Sabha but formed a coalition government with the support of some other parties. (d) Congress retained power at the Centre with an increased majority.
solution: (a) is correct. In 1967, Congress retained power at the Centre (Lok Sabha) with a reduced majority but lost Assembly elections in eight states — Bihar, UP, Punjab, Haryana, West Bengal, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan — leading to non-Congress governments there.
steps: 1967 was a watershed election — Congress won the Lok Sabha but with a greatly reduced majority (283 seats, down from 361).
Congress lost power in 8 states, including Bihar, UP, and Punjab — marking the first major challenge to Congress dominance.
Option (a) correctly describes this split outcome — Centre retained, many states lost.
Options (b), (c), and (d) are incorrect — Congress did not lose the Centre, it did form a government at the Centre, and its majority was reduced, not increased.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: Match the following: (a) Syndicate (b) Defection (c) Slogan (d) Anti-Congressism. With: i. An elected representative leaving the party on whose ticket s/he has been elected ii. A catchy phrase that attracts public attention iii. Parties with different ideological positions coming together to oppose Congress and its policies iv. A group of powerful and influential leaders within the Congress
solution: (a) Syndicate — iv. A group of powerful and influential leaders within the Congress; (b) Defection — i. An elected representative leaving the party on whose ticket s/he has been elected; (c) Slogan — ii. A catchy phrase that attracts public attention; (d) Anti-Congressism — iii. Parties with different ideological positions coming together to oppose Congress and its policies.
steps: The Syndicate was an informal group of veteran Congress leaders (Kamaraj, Nijalingappa, Morarji Desai, etc.) who controlled the party organisation.
Defection became rampant after 1967 — MLAs switched parties freely, destabilising state governments ('Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' politics).
Slogans like 'Garibi Hatao' (Indira Gandhi) and 'Indira Hatao' (opposition) were powerful electoral tools.
Anti-Congressism was Raj Narain's strategy — diverse parties uniting solely on the platform of opposing Congress.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: Whom would you identify with the following slogans/phrases? (a) Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan (b) Indira Hatao! (c) Garibi Hatao!
solution: (a) Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan — Lal Bahadur Shastri, who coined this slogan during the 1965 war to honour both soldiers and farmers. (b) Indira Hatao! — The Grand Alliance opposition in the 1971 elections, which made 'Remove Indira' its rallying cry against Indira Gandhi. (c) Garibi Hatao! — Indira Gandhi's powerful counter-slogan in the 1971 elections ('Remove Poverty'), which resonated with voters and helped Congress win a massive majority.
steps: 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan' was Shastri's call to national solidarity during the 1965 India-Pakistan war.
'Indira Hatao' was the Grand Alliance's negative campaign in 1971 — it backfired as voters saw it as elitist.
'Garibi Hatao' was Indira Gandhi's masterstroke — a positive, people-centric message that won her the 1971 election with 352 seats.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: Which of the following statements about the Grand Alliance of 1971 is correct? (a) It was formed by non-Communist, non-Congress parties. (b) It had a clear political and ideological programme. (c) It was formed by all non-Congress parties.
solution: (a) is correct. The Grand Alliance (1971) was formed by non-Communist, non-Congress parties — the Samyukta Socialists, PSP, Swatantra, Jana Sangh, and Congress(O). The Communist parties (CPI, CPI-M) did NOT join. Option (b) is incorrect — the Alliance had no positive common programme; it was united only by anti-Indira sentiment ('Indira Hatao'). Option (c) is incorrect — Communists and some regional parties did not join.
steps: The Grand Alliance united diverse non-Communist, non-Congress parties for the 1971 elections.
Its only common ground was opposing Indira Gandhi — 'Indira Hatao' was the slogan.
No positive programme or ideological unity existed — a key weakness that Indira exploited with 'Garibi Hatao'.
Communists (CPI) actually supported Indira Gandhi in 1971, not the Grand Alliance.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: How should a political party resolve its internal differences? Consider advantages and shortcomings of: (a) Follow the footsteps of the party president (b) Listen to the majority group (c) Secret ballot voting on every issue (d) Consult the senior and experienced leaders of the party
solution: (a) Following the party president: Advantage — clear leadership, decisive action. Shortcoming — authoritarian if unchecked, suppresses dissent, concentrates power. (b) Listening to the majority group: Advantage — democratic, represents the largest bloc. Shortcoming — majority can be wrong; minority views (which may be correct) are ignored. (c) Secret ballot on every issue: Advantage — each member votes freely, protects from coercion. Shortcoming — slow, impractical for a large party; may undermine party discipline and collective decision-making. (d) Consulting senior/experienced leaders: Advantage — wisdom of experience; mentorship. Shortcoming — gerontocracy; experienced leaders may be out of touch with grassroots reality.
steps: No single method is perfect — each trades off decisiveness against inclusion.
The Congress split of 1969 showed the dangers of concentrating power (Syndicate vs. Indira) AND of ignoring internal party mechanisms.
Modern democracies balance leadership authority with internal democracy through party constitutions.
The best approach usually combines regular inner-party elections, transparent debate, and final authority in the elected leadership.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: State which of these were reasons for the defeat of the Congress in 1967. Give reasons for your answer: (a) The absence of a charismatic leader (b) Split within the Congress party (c) Increased mobilisation of regional, ethnic and communal groups (d) Increasing unity among non-Congress parties (e) Internal differences within the Congress party
solution: The main reasons were (c), (d), and (e). (a) is NOT a major reason — Indira Gandhi was projected as the leader and had mass appeal; (b) is NOT correct because the formal split happened in 1969, after the 1967 elections; (c) IS correct — regional parties like DMK in Tamil Nadu and other state-level mobilisations challenged Congress; (d) IS correct — anti-Congress unity enabled coalition governments in many states; (e) IS correct — factionalism within Congress (Syndicate vs. progressives) weakened the party's electoral performance.
steps: (a) Incorrect: Indira Gandhi was the face of Congress in 1967 and remained a charismatic figure.
(b) Incorrect: The formal party split happened in 1969 (Congress-O vs. Congress-R), not before 1967 elections.
(c) Correct: DMK swept Tamil Nadu; regional parties and caste-based parties gained strength across states.
(d) Correct: Non-Congress parties united at the state level, making defection and coalition formation possible.
(e) Correct: Internal Congress divisions over ideology and leadership hurt the party's effectiveness.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: What were the factors which led to the popularity of Indira Gandhi's Government in the early 1970s?
solution: Several factors contributed: (1) The 'Garibi Hatao' slogan resonated with the poor, Dalits, minorities, and women — a new social coalition bypassing traditional Congress bosses. (2) Bank nationalisation (1969) and abolition of privy purses projected Indira as a socialist champion of the poor. (3) The victory in the 1971 Bangladesh war created a wave of national pride — Indira Gandhi was hailed as 'Durga'. (4) Winning massive state assembly elections in 1972 after Bangladesh demonstrated her national popularity. (5) Her direct communication with voters — bypassing the party organisation and appealing personally to people.
steps: 'Garibi Hatao' created a new Congress vote bank among the poor, minorities, and marginalised groups.
Bank nationalisation (1969) was a popular move seen as fighting the rich establishment.
The 1971 Bangladesh war victory made her a national hero; opposition even praised her statesmanship.
Assembly elections in early 1972 were swept by Congress — riding the post-Bangladesh patriotism wave.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: What does the term 'syndicate' mean in the context of the Congress party of the sixties? What role did the Syndicate play in the Congress party?
solution: The 'Syndicate' refers to an informal but powerful group of senior Congress leaders who controlled the party organisation in the 1960s. Key members included K. Kamaraj (Tamil Nadu), S. Nijalingappa (Karnataka), Atulya Ghosh (West Bengal), N. Sanjiva Reddy (Andhra Pradesh), and Morarji Desai. Role: The Syndicate wielded enormous power within Congress by controlling election tickets, party funds, and state party units. They were instrumental in making Indira Gandhi Prime Minister in 1966, expecting to use her as a puppet. Instead, Indira gradually bypassed the Syndicate, building her own direct mass base. The conflict between Indira and the Syndicate culminated in the 1969 Congress split — the Syndicate supported Presidential candidate N. Sanjiva Reddy, while Indira backed V.V. Giri. Giri's victory and the subsequent expulsion of the Syndicate group led to the formal split into Congress(O) and Congress(R).
steps: The Syndicate was an informal power bloc of veteran regional bosses who controlled the Congress party machine.
They made Indira Gandhi PM in 1966 hoping to control a pliable leader — their misjudgement proved historic.
Indira built a direct voter connection (especially through 'Garibi Hatao') that made her independent of the Syndicate.
The 1969 Presidential election became the flashpoint — Indira supported Giri (who won), triggering the formal Congress split.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: Discuss the major issue which led to the formal split of the Congress Party in 1969.
solution: The immediate trigger for the 1969 Congress split was the Presidential election. The Syndicate's official Congress candidate was N. Sanjiva Reddy. But Indira Gandhi covertly supported V.V. Giri (an independent candidate). Giri won. This was a direct challenge to the Syndicate's authority. The underlying issues were: (1) Ideological conflict: Indira favoured socialist policies (bank nationalisation), while the Syndicate represented the conservative establishment. (2) Power struggle: The Syndicate wanted to control Indira; she sought complete authority. The Congress Working Committee expelled Indira Gandhi in November 1969. Indira's faction (Congress-R / 'Requisitionists') became the majority Congress, while the Syndicate's Congress-O ('Organisation Congress') became a smaller splinter group.
steps: The 1969 Presidential election was the trigger — Indira backed Giri against the Syndicate's official candidate Reddy.
Giri's victory signalled Indira's independence from party bosses.
Ideological divide: bank nationalisation (July 1969) was Indira's populist move that the Syndicate's conservatives opposed.
The Syndicate expelled Indira; her parliamentary majority (with CPI, DMK support) countered that the Syndicate was the minority.
Result: Congress-R (Indira's faction) vs. Congress-O (Syndicate); Indira's faction won the 1971 elections decisively.

chapter: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System
question: Read the passage by Sudipta Kaviraj (about Indira Gandhi changing Congress from a federal, democratic formation to a centralised, undemocratic one, turning political ideology into mere electoral discourse) and answer: (a) What is the difference between the strategies of Nehru and Indira Gandhi? (b) Why does the author say that the Congress party 'died' in the seventies? (c) In what way did the change in the Congress party affect other political parties?
solution: (a) Nehru's Congress was a federal, democratic, ideological formation — it had factions, internal debate, and represented diverse social interests; ideology was taken seriously as a guide to policy. Indira Gandhi's Congress became highly centralised, dependent on the supreme leader's personal popularity, with ideology reduced to slogans ('Garibi Hatao') not translated into policy — winning elections replaced building institutions. (b) The author says Congress 'died' as a political organisation in the 1970s because it lost its capacity to function as a federal party that could absorb internal tensions and diverse interests. It became a personality cult around Indira — when she fell, the party had no independent organisational life. (c) The other parties were forced to adopt a similar style — populism, slogans, personality-centric campaigns replaced ideology and programme. This weakened institutional politics across the board and contributed to the instability of the Janata coalition (1977–79) which also lacked organisational cohesion.
steps: Nehru's Congress: ideologically serious, internally diverse, federally structured — conflict was managed within the party.
Indira's Congress: centralised, personality-driven, slogans over substance — electoral victories were its only institutional purpose.
Congress 'died' because it lost organisational autonomy and became dependent on one leader's popularity.
Other parties copied the populist style, weakening the quality of democratic politics and contributing to the Janata government's collapse.

question: State whether the following statements regarding the Emergency are correct or incorrect: (a) It was declared in 1975 by Indira Gandhi. (b) It led to the suspension of all fundamental rights. (c) It was proclaimed due to the deteriorating economic conditions. (d) Many Opposition leaders were arrested during the Emergency. (e) CPI supported the proclamation of the Emergency.
solution: (a) Correct — The Emergency was declared on 25 June 1975 by President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed on the advice of Indira Gandhi. (b) Correct — Fundamental rights including the right to move courts (Article 32) were suspended, along with free speech and personal liberty. (c) Incorrect — The official reason given was 'internal disturbance'; the actual trigger was the Allahabad High Court verdict invalidating Indira Gandhi's 1971 election. (d) Correct — JP Narayan, Morarji Desai, Atal Bihari Vajpayee, LK Advani, and thousands of others were arrested. (e) Correct — The CPI (Communist Party of India) supported the Emergency, citing the threat of a 'reactionary' RSS-backed movement.
steps: (a) Correct: Emergency proclamation signed by President on the night of 25–26 June 1975.
(b) Correct: Right to free speech, movement, and constitutional remedies were suspended; press censorship imposed.
(c) Incorrect: The real trigger was the Allahabad HC ruling against Indira; economic conditions were a background factor, not the stated reason.
(d) Correct: Mass arrests under MISA/DIR — opposition leaders, activists, and journalists were detained without trial.
(e) Correct: CPI sided with Indira, splitting the left — CPI(M) opposed the Emergency.

question: Find the odd one out in the context of the proclamation of Emergency: (a) The call for 'Total Revolution' (b) The Railway Strike of 1974 (c) The Naxalite Movement (d) The Allahabad High Court verdict (e) The findings of the Shah Commission Report
solution: (e) The findings of the Shah Commission Report is the odd one out. All the others — Total Revolution call, Railway Strike, Naxalite Movement, and Allahabad HC verdict — were cited as reasons/context for declaring the Emergency in 1975. The Shah Commission was appointed AFTER the Emergency ended (1977), by the Janata Party government, to investigate its excesses. It did not cause or contribute to the Emergency; it investigated its abuses.
steps: Items (a), (b), (c), (d) all relate to events that preceded the Emergency and were used to justify it.
JP's Total Revolution movement and student agitations destabilised Indira's government.
The 1974 Railway Strike was the largest industrial action in Indian history, projecting labour unrest.
The Allahabad HC verdict (June 1975) declared Indira's 1971 election void — the immediate trigger for Emergency.
The Shah Commission (1977–78) was a POST-Emergency enquiry — it belongs to a different time entirely.

question: Match the following: (a) Total Revolution (b) Garibi Hatao (c) Students' Protest (d) Railway Strike. With: i. Indira Gandhi ii. Jayaprakash Narayan iii. Bihar Movement iv. George Fernandes
solution: (a) Total Revolution — ii. Jayaprakash Narayan; (b) Garibi Hatao — i. Indira Gandhi; (c) Students' Protest — iii. Bihar Movement; (d) Railway Strike — iv. George Fernandes.
steps: JP Narayan's 'Total Revolution' (Sampoorna Kranti) was the umbrella idea for fundamental social, political, and economic transformation.
'Garibi Hatao' (Remove Poverty) was Indira Gandhi's 1971 election slogan that swept her to power.
The Bihar Students' Movement (1974) against corruption and price rise was the precursor to JP's national movement.
George Fernandes led the National Railway Strike of May 1974 — the largest industrial strike in Indian history.

question: What were the reasons which led to the mid-term elections in 1980?
solution: The Janata Party government (1977–79) collapsed due to internal conflicts, leading to mid-term elections in January 1980. Key reasons: (1) The Janata Party was an artificial coalition held together only by anti-Indira sentiment, lacking a common ideology or programme. (2) The RSS issue: The Janata Party split when Charan Singh and others demanded that members of the Janata with RSS backgrounds (Jana Sangh) choose between the Janata and the RSS. (3) Morarji Desai's government lost its majority in July 1979 when Charan Singh withdrew support. (4) Charan Singh then formed a government with outside support of Congress, but Congress withdrew support before he could face Parliament, and he resigned without facing a confidence vote. Fresh elections were held in January 1980, which Congress won decisively.
steps: The Janata coalition was ideologically diverse — united only by anti-Indira sentiment, not by any positive programme.
The RSS controversy split the coalition — Socialists and Charan Singh's faction demanded Jana Sangh members cut RSS ties.
Morarji Desai lost his majority in July 1979; Charan Singh formed a government but could not face Parliament.
Congress withdrew support from Charan Singh before he could prove his majority; President's Rule and fresh elections followed.

question: The Shah Commission was appointed in 1977 by the Janata Party Government. Why was it appointed and what were its findings?
solution: The Shah Commission (headed by Justice J.C. Shah, former Chief Justice of India) was appointed to inquire into the excesses committed during the Emergency (1975–77). Findings: (1) The Emergency was constitutionally valid but politically motivated — declared primarily to save Indira Gandhi from the consequences of the Allahabad HC verdict. (2) Mass arrests: Thousands were detained without legal recourse; many were tortured. (3) Press censorship was total and politically partisan — not national security driven. (4) Forced sterilisations during the family planning programme caused immense suffering. (5) The 20-point economic programme had some merit but was implemented coercively. (6) Individual officials and politicians who exceeded their authority were identified. The Commission's reports documented the abuse of power comprehensively.
steps: The Shah Commission was the official post-Emergency accountability mechanism appointed by the Janata government.
Its mandate: investigate Emergency declaration, arrests, censorship, and other excesses.
Findings: politically motivated declaration; mass arbitrary detention; torture; total press censorship.
The forced sterilisation drive (Sanjay Gandhi's programme) was a major documented atrocity.
The Commission identified responsible officials but no major prosecutions followed under subsequent governments.

question: What reasons did the Government give for declaring a National Emergency in 1975?
solution: The official reason given by the Indira Gandhi government for declaring the Emergency on 25 June 1975 was the existence of 'internal disturbance' threatening India's security (under Article 352 of the Constitution). The government claimed that the country faced a threat from the JP movement, which was allegedly inciting the army and police to disobey orders. The Allahabad High Court verdict (June 1975) invalidating Indira Gandhi's 1971 election win was the real trigger, but the government framed the Emergency as necessary to save democracy from the destabilising forces of the opposition movement. The term 'internal disturbance' was later changed to 'armed rebellion' by the 44th Constitutional Amendment to make Emergency declarations harder to justify.
steps: Official reason: 'internal disturbance' threatening national security under Article 352.
Government claimed JP's movement was inciting police and army to disobey orders.
Real trigger: Allahabad HC verdict of 12 June 1975 voiding Indira's 1971 election win for electoral malpractice.
Indira refused to resign and instead declared Emergency to prevent her removal from office.
The 44th Amendment later tightened Emergency provisions to prevent misuse.

question: The 1977 elections for the first time saw the Opposition coming into power at the Centre. What would you consider as the reasons for this development?
solution: Several factors explain the 1977 opposition victory: (1) Anti-Emergency sentiment: The Emergency period (1975–77) saw repression — mass arrests, press censorship, forced sterilisations — that created widespread public anger. (2) Unity of opposition: All major non-Communist parties merged into the Janata Party, avoiding vote splits. (3) JP's leadership: Jayaprakash Narayan was a widely respected, non-partisan figure who gave the movement moral authority. (4) Rural anger: Forced sterilisations disproportionately targeted poor rural communities, alienating Congress's traditional vote bank. (5) North India swing: The Hindi-belt states (UP, Bihar, Rajasthan, MP, Haryana) swung decisively against Congress, giving Janata huge majorities. (6) Indira's miscalculation: She called elections expecting to win, misjudging public mood after 21 months of censored media.
steps: Anti-Emergency public anger was the primary driver — people resented arrests, censorship, and forced sterilisations.
Opposition unity (merging into one Janata Party) eliminated the vote-splitting that had previously helped Congress.
JP's moral authority gave the movement broad legitimacy across ideological lines.
North Indian rural voters — hit hardest by sterilisation campaigns — turned against Congress en masse.

question: Discuss the effects of Emergency on: (a) Civil liberties for citizens (b) Relationship between the Executive and Judiciary (c) Functioning of Mass Media (d) Working of the Police and Bureaucracy
solution: (a) Civil liberties: Fundamental rights including personal liberty (Article 21), free speech (Article 19), and constitutional remedies (Article 32) were suspended. Citizens could be detained without trial under MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act). Habeas corpus petitions were dismissed by the Supreme Court (ADM Jabalpur case — a controversial judgment). (b) Executive-Judiciary: The executive clearly dominated. The Supreme Court's ADM Jabalpur judgment (1976) held that even the right to life could be suspended during Emergency — a major blow to judicial independence. Transfers and supersessions of judges who ruled against the government increased. (c) Mass Media: Complete press censorship was imposed; newspapers had to submit copy for approval before publication. Several newspapers like The Indian Express resisted. The Emergency demonstrated the media's vulnerability to political control. (d) Police and Bureaucracy: Police acted with impunity — mass arrests without warrants, torture in custody, and targeting of opposition workers. Bureaucracy became highly politicised, implementing Emergency directives without question. The Sanjay Gandhi coterie operated as an extra-constitutional power centre directing officials.
steps: Civil liberties: MISA detentions without trial; Article 32 suspended; Supreme Court (ADM Jabalpur) held right to life could be suspended.
Executive-Judiciary: ADM Jabalpur case was the judiciary's low point; judges were transferred for unfavourable rulings.
Mass Media: Total pre-publication censorship; newspapers blank-fronted or ran editorials of solidarity; overseas papers' distribution was stopped.
Police/Bureaucracy: Extra-legal detention and torture; Sanjay Gandhi wielded informal but real power over administrators and police.

question: In what way did the imposition of Emergency affect the party system in India? Elaborate your answer with examples.
solution: The Emergency had lasting effects on India's party system: (1) Congress split further: After the 1977 defeat, Congress itself split — Indira Gandhi's group became Congress(I), while others remained in the old Congress. (2) Opposition consolidation: For the first time, multiple parties — Jana Sangh, BLD, Congress(O), Socialists — merged to form the Janata Party, showing that opposition unity was possible. (3) Delegitimisation of authoritarian politics: The Emergency experience made future declarations politically very costly. No Emergency has been imposed since. (4) JP movement's legacy: The Janata experiment, though short-lived, showed that ideologically diverse coalitions were possible but difficult to sustain. (5) Rise of new parties: After Janata's collapse, the BJP (founded 1980 from Jana Sangh) and other regional parties emerged, accelerating the move towards coalition politics.
steps: Congress split post-1977 defeat: Congress(I) under Indira vs. older Congress factions.
The Janata experiment showed opposition unity was achievable but ideological differences made it unsustainable.
Emergency became politically illegitimate — no government has dared use Article 352 for internal reasons since 1977.
BJP emerged in 1980 from the Jana Sangh component of Janata — the Emergency experience shaped its political identity.
The coalition era that fully flowered in the 1990s had its roots in the anti-Emergency unity of 1977.

question: Read the passage by Partha Chatterjee (on India being close to a two-party system in 1977 elections, then splitting into many parties) and answer: (a) What made the party system in India look like a two-party system in 1977? (b) Many more than two parties existed in 1977. Why then are the authors describing this period as close to a two-party system? (c) What caused splits in Congress and the Janata parties?
solution: (a) In 1977, the contest was essentially bipolar: the unified Janata Party versus the Congress, with most voters and parties choosing one of these two camps. The merger of Jana Sangh, BLD, Congress(O), Socialists, and CFD into one Janata Party created a single anti-Congress pole, making the election appear like a two-party contest. (b) Although multiple parties existed, they had all merged into or aligned with one of just two main formations — Janata (on one side) and Congress (on the other). Small parties and regional parties mostly fell into one of these two camps. The effective choice for voters was binary — hence the 'near two-party' description. (c) Congress split: After the 1977 defeat, personal ambitions, disagreements over Indira Gandhi's leadership, and the 1978 elections caused Congress to split into Congress(I) under Indira and other Congress factions. Janata split: The Janata Party had no common ideology — it was an anti-Emergency coalition. The RSS controversy, personal rivalries (Morarji vs. Charan Singh), and loss of the common enemy (the Emergency) led to its rapid fragmentation.
steps: (a) 1977 was bipolar: All major opposition parties merged into Janata, creating a two-camp contest — Janata vs. Congress.
(b) Near two-party system: even though many parties existed, they all chose sides — Janata camp or Congress camp.
(c) Congress split: post-defeat recriminations, Indira's leadership style, and 1978 state elections caused Congress(I) vs. other Congress.
(c) Janata split: no shared ideology beyond anti-Emergency; RSS controversy; Morarji vs. Charan Singh rivalry; power struggles.
